newsitem.title: UK: UK stocks outlook - Budget jitters continue.
newsitem.headline: UK stocks outlook - Budget jitters continue.

text.p: Fears over the contents of the July 2 British budget are likely to keep on the London equity market on edge next week, investment strategists said on Friday.

This week the market lost about four percent in five straight declines amid worries that the new Labour government's first budget will cut tax breaks that have the effect of boosting the value of shares to some of the market's biggest investors - the pension funds.
Yet if Chancellor (finance minster) Gordon Brown takes the radical option of abolishing the tax credit, the impact on the equities market could be a lot harsher.
One strategist said the FTSE 100 index of top companies could drop as low as 4,400 points if the tax credit was ditched -- some 200 points below Friday's close.
"If they scrap the ACT (advanced corporation tax) relief we will go down to that level, but no further," he said.

Economic data, including UK economic growth in the first quarter of the year, could also be a focus of concern, compounding mounting worries that further bullish economic data will lead to more interest rate increases.
However, the budget watch is likely to capture the most attention.
Under the current system, pension funds are exempt from taxes and can therefore reclaim the 20 percent ACT that companies pay on dividends.
Since pension funds own almost the half shares in the UK equity market, shares prices theoretically could drop by about 10 percent if the concession is removed.
It was a report in the Financial Times on June 16 that raised fears over the tax credit, terminating a rally in the FTSE 100 that carried the blue chip index to a record 4,796.0 on June 13.

There is a risk that if Brown targets most of his tax-raising measures on the corporate sector, he will be passing up the chance of a squeeze on consumers that could have eased pressure for higher interest rates.

Analysts said the Bank of England was likely to progressively tighten credit to curb booming consumer spending -- highlighted by last week's figures showing a stronger-than-expected 1.1 percent rise in May retail sales -- unless fiscal measures were taken.
"The Budget and the fear of higher rates will keep the FTSE 100 under a cloud," said Robert Buckland, strategist at brokerage HSBC James Capel.
Yet some said the complete abolition of the tax credit remained unlikely. Anyway, much of the impact of its elimination should already have been factored in to share prices.
Ian Williams, strategist at Panmure Gordon, saw the FTSE going down to 4,500 at worst. "All this has been talked about enough," he said. "A big part of all that is already in the price."
